tools.name: wait
tools.description:
Waits on a yielded `exec` cell and returns new output or completion.
- Use `wait` only after `exec` returns `Script running with cell ID ...`.
- `cell_id` identifies the running `exec` cell to resume.
- `yield_time_ms` controls how long to wait for more output before yielding again. Defaults to 10000 ms.
- `max_tokens` limits how much new output this wait call returns. Defaults to 10000 tokens.
- `terminate: true` stops the running cell; false or omitted waits for output.
- `wait` returns only the new output since the last yield, or the final completion or termination result for that cell.
- If the cell is still running, `wait` may yield again with the same `cell_id`.
- If the cell has already finished, `wait` returns the completed result and closes the cell.

cell_id.description: Identifier of the running exec cell.

max_tokens.description: Output token budget for this wait call. Defaults to 10000 tokens.

terminate.description: True stops the running exec cell; false or omitted waits for output.

yield_time_ms.description: Wait before yielding more output. Defaults to 10000 ms.

- `gpt-6.2-sol`: Fast, go-to model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6.2-astra`: Our most capable model for complex coding and professional work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6.1-terra`: Efficient model that excels at visual understanding and computer use. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6.1-sol`: Previous generation model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6-astra`: Previous generation model for complex coding and professional work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
        Spawns an agent to work on the specified task. If your current task is `/root/task1` and you spawn_agent with task_name "task_3" the agent will have canonical task name `/root/task1/task_3`.
You are then able to refer to this agent as `task_3` or `/root/task1/task_3` interchangeably. However an agent `/root/task2/task_3` would only be able to communicate with this agent via its canonical name `/root/task1/task_3`.
The spawned agent will have the same tools as you and the ability to spawn its own subagents.

It will be able to send you and other running agents messages, and its final answer will be provided to you when it finishes.
The new agent's canonical task name will be provided to it along with the message.

Note that passing `fork_turns="none"` will not pass any surrounding context to the spawned subagent, which may cause the agent to lack the context it needs to complete its task, whereas `fork_turns="all"` will provide the subagent with all surrounding context.

fork_turns.description: Parent history to inherit. Defaults to `all`; use `none` to start without parent history. Only `all` and `none` are supported.

model.description: Model override for the new agent. Omit unless an explicit override is needed.

tools.name: js
tools.description:
Control native apps or browsers on the user’s computer by reading or operating UI. Prefer purpose-built skills, connectors, APIs, or CLIs when available.

On the first invocation of `cua_repl`, or after resetting it, execute exactly one of the API calls shown below, optionally assigning its result to a variable. Do not add other API calls, waits, or snapshots to that invocation.
The tool result will include documentation and, when creating or selecting a tab or selecting an app, its initial UI state. Selecting a browser does not open a tab. Read that result before continuing.
Use only APIs described in the tool instructions or returned documentation.

When you need an inventory of available apps, browsers, and tabs, get a snapshot of all enabled surfaces. Otherwise, use the relevant entry point below:

```javascript
await cua.getState();
```

Use the first matching browser control option from the user's request:

For a tab @-mention (`mention=tab-v1`):
Pass the complete `plugin://...` URL to get the referenced tab.

```javascript
let tab = await cua.getTab({ mention: tabMentionUrl });
```

For an existing tab identified by URL in browser context (including the current IAB tab):

```javascript
let tab = await cua.getTab({ url }, { browser: browserId });
```

Known tab ID (`tabId` or `providerTabId`) and browser (name or browser @-mention):

```javascript
let tab = await cua.getTab(tabId, { browser: browserId });
```

To open a URL in the in-app browser (`@Browser`):

```javascript
let tab = await cua.createBrowserTab("iab", url, { visible: boolean });
```

To open a URL in another named browser: pass its name directly; do not call `getBrowser` first.

```javascript
let tab = await cua.createBrowserTab(browserName, url, browserOptions);
```

Known URL, only when the user has not specified a browser by name or @-mention:

```javascript
let browser = await cua.getBrowser({ url });
```

Browser IDs and options:

- `"mcpapps"`: use `cua.getBrowser({ id: "mcpapps" })` for existing full-screen MCP Apps in the task’s side panel.
- `"iab"` (in-app browser): in `createBrowserTab`, use `visible: true` to show the browser; `false` to keep it hidden.
- `"dot"` (Dot): use only when present in browser inventory. It accesses tabs on Dot's active main thread. `cua.getTab(tabId, { browser: "dot" })` selects an existing tab. `cua.createBrowserTab("dot", url, { visible: boolean })` creates one with the same visibility options as `"iab"`.
- `"chrome"` (@Chrome), `"edge"` (@Edge): pass a short, emoji-prefixed `sessionName` (e.g. `"🔎 Task"`) to `createBrowserTab` when starting a task.

If the user specifies an app to use, get the app by name, bundle ID, or path:

```javascript
let app = await cua.getApp("Example App");
```

To add other content to the tool result, use `nodeRepl.write(value)` for text or other values and `await nodeRepl.emitImage(image)` for images. The APIs listed above already display their documentation or UI state; do not wrap their results in `write` or `emitImage`.

If your context begins with a summary of an existing computer use task, call `await cua.rewriteDocumentation()` before continuing the computer use task to ensure you have a complete view of the necessary documentation.

Several `cua_repl.js` calls may work toward the same goal. As soon as you observe the final outcome of the CUA part of the task, make your next tool call `cua_repl.js` with only `completion_summary`, exactly once. Do this before using another tool for the next part of the user’s request or sending your reply, even if the overall request continues. If you hand control to the user, wait to summarize until the handoff has ended and you’ve observed the final outcome of the CUA part of the task. This tool is part of plugin `unified-computer-use`.

# Project Management

The [LibreLift MVP project board](https://github.com/orgs/LibreLift/projects/1)
tracks planned work, priorities, and progress. Use the Plan view to see task sizes
and milestone groupings, and the Backlog view to follow workflow states. Check
the view's filters if an expected issue is not visible.

## Requests and triage

Use the repository's issue templates to report a problem, suggest a feature, or
request a documentation change. Feature and bug templates apply `needs triage`;
a request is not a commitment to implement it.

Maintainers review requests for scope, clarity, duplicates, and dependencies.
They ask for missing context, explain decisions on the issue, and either close
the request with a reason, defer it, or turn accepted work into actionable tasks.
Only maintainers apply `planned work`, so contributors can distinguish agreed
work from requests still under discussion. When a broad request is replaced by
smaller tasks, link the replacements and explain that closing the request does
not mean its implementation is complete.

## Planned work, epics, and milestones

Use the Task template for agreed work. Each task should describe its goal,
context and related design links, checkable acceptance criteria, dependencies,
and where to start. Size tasks with the board's Task Size field: XS is up to
one hour, S is two hours, M is four hours, L is seven hours, and XL is more than
seven hours. Split work that contains independently useful, reviewable changes.

Group feature tasks under a parent issue labeled `epic`, using GitHub
sub-issues. Epics describe user-visible outcomes; shared setup tasks can remain
standalone when several epics depend on them. Link dependencies so contributors
can see what must be finished first.

Assign planned work to the milestone it supports:

- **M1: Runnable Demo — November 18, 2026:** account access, exercise selection,
  and creating, saving, reopening, editing, and deleting fixed-weight templates.
- **M2: MVP — December 2, 2026:** workout logging and history, personal exercise
  maximums, percentage-based targets, and deferred catalog caching/retry work.

The M1 milestone description records capacity, estimates, and scope cuts.
Maintainers keep milestone assignments and board priorities aligned with that
budget. See the [roadmap](./roadmap.md) for work beyond the MVP.

## Workflow states

| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Backlog | Work is recorded but is not ready to start. |
| Ready | Scope and acceptance criteria are clear and prerequisites are available. |
| In progress | An assigned contributor is actively working on the issue. |
| In review | The implementation PR is ready for independent review. |
| Done | The change has met the [definition of done](./git-standards.md#definition-of-done). |

Keep issue and board status current as work moves. A blocked task should not be
treated as ready until its prerequisites are resolved. Closed requests that were
superseded or declined should be distinguished from completed implementation in
their closing explanation.

templates and workout sessions.

**Account**:
The identity through which a user signs in and accesses their saved training data.
_Avoid_: User when referring specifically to sign-in identity

**Account name**:
The name a user chooses to display for their account. It can be changed without
changing the email address used to sign in.
_Avoid_: Username when implying a unique sign-in identifier

### Planning

**Exercise**:
A movement, such as a bench press or squat, described by its name, target muscles,
and equipment.

**Exercise catalog**:
The collection of exercises available for inclusion in workout templates.
_Avoid_: Workout catalog, template library

**Catalog exercise**:
A named movement in the exercise catalog, with an identity shared by every template
or session that references it.
_Avoid_: Template exercise, session exercise

**Primary muscles**:
The muscles identified by the catalog as the main targets of an exercise. Missing
targets remain unspecified rather than being inferred.
_Avoid_: All target muscles

**Secondary muscles**:
The muscles identified by the catalog as supporting targets of an exercise,
distinct from its primary muscles. Missing targets remain unspecified rather than
being inferred.
_Avoid_: Primary muscles

**Muscle group**:
A broader category of muscles described by a familiar training label, such as
Chest, Upper back, Lower back, or Calves.
_Avoid_: Primary muscle when referring to the broader category

**No equipment**:
An exercise's explicit lack of required equipment, identified from the catalog's
bodyweight designation when equipment is absent. Missing equipment without that
designation is not evidence that no equipment is required.
_Avoid_: Unknown equipment

**Workout template**:
A reusable workout description containing exercises and their planned sets.
“Template” is its short name.
_Avoid_: Plan, routine (as separate domain concepts)

**Template draft**:
Unsaved changes to a workout template. These changes are separate from the saved
template until the user saves them.

**Template exercise**:
A placement of a catalog exercise within a workout template, with its own identity,
saved exercise details, and planned sets. The same catalog exercise can appear in
multiple placements; catalog changes do not change saved templates.
_Avoid_: Exercise when referring specifically to its inclusion in a template

**Template set**:
A planned set for a template exercise, with a target weight and target repetition
count.
_Avoid_: Round

### Performing and reviewing

**Workout session**:
One occurrence of performing a workout based on a workout template. “Session” is
its short name.
_Avoid_: Workout when the distinction from a workout template matters

**Session exercise**:
A placement of a catalog exercise within a workout session, with its own identity,
saved exercise details, and session sets. Its catalog identity is retained, and
catalog changes do not change saved workout history.
_Avoid_: Template exercise when referring to a session's exercise

**Session set**:
A set belonging to a session exercise, with planned targets and the performance
recorded for that session.
_Avoid_: Round, template set when referring to a session's set

**Workout history**:
The collection of saved past workout sessions available for review.
_Avoid_: Workout log, log (as names for a separate domain concept)

### Sets and performance

**Repetition**:
One performance of an exercise's movement. “Rep” is its short name.

**Set**:
A group of repetitions of one exercise; it belongs to that exercise rather than
grouping several exercises together.
_Avoid_: Round, circuit

**Target performance**:
The planned weight and repetition count for a set.
_Avoid_: Goal when referring specifically to a set's targets

**Fixed-weight target**:
A target weight expressed directly as an amount of weight.

**Personal exercise maximum**:
The weight a user records as their maximum for one repetition of a particular
exercise. It is the reference weight for percentage-based targets.

**Percentage-based target**:
A target weight expressed as a percentage of the user's personal maximum for that
exercise.

**Recorded performance**:
The weight and repetition count recorded for a session set, which may differ from
its target performance. “Actual” is a synonym for these recorded values.

# LibreLift roadmap

LibreLift provides free workout planning and logging for individual users. This
roadmap follows the project proposal's feature priorities: P0 is the minimum viable
product (MVP), P1 is the next step, and P2 is longer-term exploration. Work after
the MVP has no committed release dates.

## MVP

The semester MVP lets a user create and reuse workout templates using exercises
from a catalog, start workout sessions using existing templates, and review saved
workout history. It also supports recording exercise maximums and calculating
target weights as percentages of those maximums. These functions are available
without a subscription or payment.

The MVP is scoped to two delivery milestones:

| Milestone | Target date | What a user can do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [M1: Runnable Demo](https://github.com/LibreLift/libre-lift/milestone/1) | November 18, 2026 | Sign in, choose catalog exercises, and create, save, reopen, edit, and delete a workout template with fixed target weights and repetitions. Workout logging and maximum-based calculations are deferred to M2. |
| [M2: MVP](https://github.com/LibreLift/libre-lift/milestone/2) | December 2, 2026 | Start a workout from a saved template, record actual weights and repetitions, complete or stop the workout, and review its saved history. Record personal exercise maximums and use percentages to calculate template target weights. |

Templates and workout history must persist across app restarts. Editing or reusing
a template must not alter previously logged workouts. The first milestone covers
the complete template-creation workflow; the second adds the workout-logging
workflow and percentage-based planning.

The features below are deferred from the MVP to keep the semester build focused
on these core workflows within the available development time. Contributors can
help with implementation, testing, and documentation; see the
[contribution guide](../CONTRIBUTING.md) and
[project board](https://github.com/orgs/LibreLift/projects/1) for how to get involved
and what work is currently planned.

## Next

These P1 features extend the MVP once the core planning and logging workflows
are established. Their order below follows the CP3 proposal.

1. **Integrated rest timer.** Add a rest timer to the workout experience. This is
   next because it improves an existing workflow without introducing a separate
   product area. It is deferred from the MVP because a timer is not required to
   record a workout. Contributors can help design the controls, implement the
   timer, and test it during workout sessions.
2. **Visual aids for past workout statistics.** Add visualizations of saved workout
   history so users can understand progress over time. This follows basic history
   viewing because the app first needs reliable workout records. Advanced visuals
   are deferred from the MVP, which provides the underlying logs. Contributors
   can help identify useful statistics and build and test their visualizations.

## Later

These P2 features are exploratory ideas from the project proposal. They follow the
MVP and P1 improvements because they expand the app from recording user-created
plans into suggesting plans and starting workouts without an exiting plan, requiring additional design and validation.

1. **Generate one-off workouts or workout plans.** Help users assemble a one-off workouts
   rather than requiring them to create or select a plan. Generated workouts can then be saved as a new template if desired. This is
   deferred until the exercise catalog and template workflows are established.
   Contributors can help define generation rules and check that generated plans
   use the catalog and fit the existing template model.
2. **Suggest workouts for fitness goals or sports training.** Explore suggestions
   tailored to a user's stated goal or sport. This is deferred because the proposal
   identifies a need for more evidence about what users want from planning.
   Contributors can help research those needs, define the supported goals, and
   evaluate suggestions before implementation.

## Not planned

These non-goals from the proposal remain outside the current plan. They are
excluded to protect the semester scope and the focus on individual workout
planning and logging.

- **Nutrition or macro tracking.** This introduces a separate problem area and
  would stretch the project beyond the available build time.
- **Body composition and fitness goal customization.** Automatically prescribing
  workouts, repetitions, or weights using body-profile information such as gender,
  height, and weight is outside the semester scope. The exploratory goal- or
  sport-based suggestions in Later do not commit the project to this broader
  personalization system.
- **Social exercising features.** Friends, followers, workout sharing, comments,
  and cooperative workout logging are excluded because the project prioritizes
  meeting individual users' needs independently.

## 1. Context and scope

LibreLift is a native mobile app for planning, logging, and tracking workouts for those who want to use their phones to do so. It aims to provide the basic functions of creating reusable workout templates, using a template for a workout and logging reps and weight, and reviewing the details of past workouts. For more information about the context of this project, see the [proposal document](../cp3/cp3-proposal).

- Support starting, stopping, and completing workout sessions for an existing template. Workout sessions allow recording repetitions performed and weight used for each session exercise.
- Support storing "one-rep" maximum weight for certain exercises, and enter weight in template exercises as a percentage of that maximum.

### Core flow - Making a workout template

1. A user logs in or signs up with credentials
2. User taps the screen to create a workout template
3. View layer sends input to ViewModel
4. ViewModel navigates to template creator business logic, calls service to load catalog
5. Service calls the Exercise CDN to load catalog, returns data to ViewModel
6. ViewModel sends exercises to View

15. HTTPHandler receives workout template JSON, passes to DataAccess layer via function call
16. DataAccess layer deserializes JSON, writes to DB via HTTP

### The failure case

1. User taps the screen to create a workout template
2. View layer sends input to ViewModel
3. ViewModel navigates to template creator business logic, calls service to load catalog
4. Service checks if the catalog is cached. If not, call the Service layer
5. Service calls the Exercise CDN to load catalog, returns data to ViewModel
6. CDN throws an error and does not return catalog
7. Service passes an error to the ViewModel layer
8. ViewModel layer formats the error message to display on the UI
9. UI displays the error message for the User, asks to wait for a period and then try again

### Core flow - Logging a workout:

1. A user logs in using credentials
2. User selects one of their templates and taps  a "Start workout" button.
3. A stopwatch/counter displays workout duration, and lists the exercises in the workout.
4. For each exercise, the user is able to tap it and see a detailed view 
5. The user can adjust actual weight and reps used if it differs from the templated amounts
6. After performing a set of one exercise, the user marks that set complete.
7. This is repeated for the planned sets of each exercise; the MVP does not group exercises into circuit rounds.
8. When finished, the user taps "Finish workout"
9. The workout session is completed and added to the user's workout history
10. The user can navigate to workout history and see the details of their session

### The failure case

1. A user logs in using credentials
2. User selects one of their templates and taps  a "Start workout" button.
3. The user proceeds through the workout as stated above
4. When tapping the "Finish workout" button, the DB write fails
5. The error message is sent back to the user and told to try again in a few minutes.
6. If the error persists a second time, the user is presented a button to send feedback.
7. The feedback link sends an email to the maintainers with the user input.

### M1 database scope and account data (#102)

See the [confirmed #102 specification](./issue-102-database.md) for acceptance
criteria, implementation boundaries, and the approved database testing seam.

The M1 database includes an application-owned User table, workout templates,
template exercises, and template sets. Workout sessions, session exercises,
session sets, personal exercise maximums, and percentage-based targets are added
through later migrations for M2; the table above describes the broader MVP model.

The application-owned User table stores the editable account name and uses the
Supabase Auth account's ID as its identity. Training records reference this
application User for ownership and relationships. The account name is a display
name, not a unique sign-in identifier. This decision replaces #42's use of Auth
user metadata for the account name. Do not add application columns to or otherwise
alter Supabase's managed Auth schema; Supabase Auth continues to manage credentials
and authentication sessions.

After email verification, an authenticated account-data read loads the application
User if one exists. An absent User requires name onboarding without creating a
row. Submitting a valid account name creates the User with the Auth account's ID;
a failed save preserves the entered name for retry. Existing Users load their
stored account name. Account access integration in #42 must follow this flow.

If email-code verification succeeds but the application User lookup fails, retain
the verified authentication session in memory and keep training screens gated.
Show an actionable error with **Retry loading account**, which retries only the
User lookup, without requesting or verifying another code. Appearance Settings
remains available. Only a successful lookup with no User opens name onboarding;
a lookup failure remains in the retry state. This recovery is part of #42;
authentication restoration and lifecycle are specified below.

Template exercises store their placement identity, namespaced catalog identity,
parent template, and position relationally. Each placement also stores a complete
descriptive JSON snapshot, including name, distinct primary and secondary muscles,
equipment, and available images, instructions, and translations. Template sets
remain relational. Saved detail reads these snapshots without consulting the live
catalog; #102 does not import a shared exercise catalog table. This implements the
existing catalog identity and snapshot decision rather than treating the ERD's
Exercise entity as a live source of saved descriptions.

Authenticated database requests use the requesting account's context so row-level
security applies. Explicit grants and policies allow only owner-scoped access to
application User and template data; anonymous access is denied. Backend operations
must not routinely bypass these policies with a privileged service credential.
Deleting a template cascades to its placements and sets. Deleting an Auth account
cascades to its application User and owned templates. Users cannot change their
identity or transfer ownership. An account-deletion UI remains outside M1 scope.

Saved templates and template-exercise placements use UUID identities. Placement
identity remains unchanged when exercises move; a separate numeric position
records order. Template sets use numbers within their placement. Templates store
creation timestamps for stable list ordering. Draft identity conversion belongs
to #45's persistence integration.

Database constraints enforce valid relationships, nonblank names, nonnegative
finite decimal weights in pounds, positive integer target repetitions, and unique
exercise positions and set numbers within their parents. Issue #45 validates and
saves a complete template atomically, including at least one exercise, at least
one set per exercise, and consecutive ordering. Multirow edits may temporarily
have incomplete structure within their transaction.

Issue #102's primary verification seam is the real local Supabase database, using
anonymous and two authenticated identities. Tests verify allowed operations,
ownership isolation and attempted ownership changes, invalid values, snapshots,
ordering, and deletion cascades. Migrations must rebuild cleanly and apply to a
populated database without losing existing records. App-flow verification remains
with #42 and #45. Deliver locally verified migrations and hosted deployment
instructions; applying them to the shared hosted backend follows the existing
post-review maintainer workflow. Do not automatically seed user data or sample
templates.

Issue #102 owns the M1 schema, relationship constraints, access grants, row-level
security, and database verification. Issue #45 builds template persistence
operations and app integration on that foundation; #43 owns authentication-session
restoration. Valid stored authentication is restored automatically, while explicit
sign-out or an app reinstall requires another email OTP. Saved templates belong
to the account and survive app reloads, restarts, updates, and reinstalls when
using the same backend. Unsaved template drafts remain temporary.

### Template persistence (#45)

The [confirmed #45 specification](./issue-45-template-persistence.md) governs the
implemented production template service; hosted deployment and device audit remain
separate review activities. Whole-template
saves use an authenticated Edge Function/data-access boundary and an invoker-rights
transactional database function; see [ADR 0005](./adr/0005-save-template-aggregates-transactionally.md).
An unchanged save retry recovers its original committed result without duplicate
creation or overwriting later saves. Distinct concurrent saves use last-committed

## 6. Technology choices and alternatives considered

### Decision: What ExerciseDB/CDN will be used

- **Chosen:** RepDB
- **Alternative considered:** yuhonas/free-exercise-db
- **Why the chosen option wins, given our goals:** There is a free starter license, and the example images are superior than those in free-exercise-db
- **Evidence:** The spike utilized RepDB, while a personal side project has utilized free-exercise-db, and the RepDB images are superior, while muscle grouping, exercises available, and instructions are roughly equivalent.
- **What would change our mind:** If the user base grows enough that the RepDB free license is no longer usable, I would want to switch to the free alternative of free-exercise-db
### Decision: Which Backend as a Service (BaaS) technology will be used?

- **Chosen**: Supabase
- **Alternative considered**: Firebase
- **Why the chosen option wins, given our goals**: 2 main reasons: First, Supabase is better build for open-source contributions, since contributors can run a local version of the backend without needing access to the production credentials. Second, the data model for LibreLift (workouts, exercises, template vs session) fits well in a relational model, which is more readily available in Supabase. One advantage that Firebase does have is out of the box support for offline-synchronization.
- **Evidence**: The Supabase CLI allows any developer to run backend services locally with one command (`npx supabase start`). This is a huge asset for an open-source project. Supabase is naturally relational with PostgreSQL, and Firebase is natively NoSQL. Firebase does support SQL using SQL Connect, which requires some additional configuration. Offline synchronization is possible with Supabase, but requires more manual configuration than Firebase.
- **What would change our mind**: If offline synchronization became too complex with Supabase, switching to Firebase would become a real consideration. Or, if the scale of the project grows enough and pricing between Supabase and Firebase favor Firebase, that would also merit considering a switch.

### Decision: What authentication method will be used

**Chosen**: Email OTP only.
**Alternatives considered**: Email + password, email magic link, Google OAuth, Apple OAuth.
**Why the chosen option wins, given our goals**: Users are expected to sign in infrequently and remain signed in on their device. Email OTP avoids managing a rarely used password and the configuration overhead of OAuth providers.
**Evidence**: Supabase supports email OTP for new and returning users and renewable sessions without a default maximum lifetime. During the Issue #42 design discussion, this approach was selected based on the expected infrequency of sign-ins for a gym app. The expectation is that users will sign in once and then use the app as desired.
**What would change our mind**: Evidence that users need another sign-in method.

See [ADR 0004: Use email OTP for account access](./adr/0004-email-otp-account-access.md)
for the agreed account-access behavior, session boundary, and testing decisions.

## Problem Statement

LibreLift stores Supabase credentials on the device but does not restore them into application state when the app launches. Returning users must repeat account access, and the app does not yet respond to session lifecycle changes or provide sign-out.

Training services, cached reads, and unfinished work can outlive protected routes. Simply returning to email entry would therefore leave the previous account's state available in memory. Users need reliable returning access and a clear boundary that prevents one account's state from appearing under another account.

## Solution

Restore usable stored authentication behind a loading gate, load the application User, and enter the app only after any required account-name onboarding. Keep sessions renewable without an application-imposed maximum lifetime or inactivity timeout.

Routine same-account token refresh preserves ongoing work. When authentication becomes unusable, gate training. Temporary failures offer recovery without erasing stored authentication; successful recovery starts with a clean load and discards drafts and navigation. Definitively invalid authentication clears account-specific state and returns to email access.

Provide device-local sign-out. Clear account-specific services, caches, edits, drafts, and navigation when authentication ends or the account changes, and prevent late responses from repopulating them. Preserve device appearance preferences and saved backend data.

## User Stories

1. As a returning user, I want valid stored authentication restored when I launch the app, so that I do not need another email code.
2. As a user, I want a loading screen while restoration is unresolved, so that I understand why training is not yet available.

# Use MVVM with injected asynchronous services

For [#38](https://github.com/LibreLift/libre-lift/issues/38), UI stubs need to behave
like clients of real data while backend features are still being built. Views
therefore render ViewModel state, and ViewModels consume injected asynchronous
service interfaces; the app's root supplies sample data and preference-storage
implementations. This adds a small amount of boundary code compared with embedding
fixtures in screens, but allows service integration and controlled failure testing
without coupling the views to either fixtures or backend clients.
# Preserve session history independently of templates

The [roadmap](../roadmap.md#mvp) requires template edits and reuse to leave earlier
workout sessions unchanged. Session exercises, target performance, and recorded
performance therefore belong to the session independently of the editable
template, accepting duplicated values instead of reconstructing history from the
current template. The current sample records demonstrate this separation; session
creation and backend persistence remain future feature work.
# Separate exercise placements from catalog identity and preserve saved details

Template and session exercise placements have their own identifiers while retaining the same catalog identifier for the movement they reference. Saved templates and sessions preserve exercise details rather than resolving them from the current external catalog, so repeated placements remain distinct and upstream renames or removals cannot alter saved workouts. This accepts duplicated descriptive data in exchange for stable saved plans and history.

Catalog identifiers include a provider namespace, such as `repdb:bench-press`, to prevent accidental identity collisions if another catalog is introduced. Equivalent movements from different providers require an explicit mapping; matching names or provider-local identifiers do not establish equivalence.

## Round 1

❓ **Q1 — Is one device the product model?** If someone logs a workout on their phone and opens the app on a tablet that evening, are you comfortable with each device having its own workout history? Is that a deliberate product choice or a concession to ship the MVP?

➡️ **My recommendation:** Make a single device the supported MVP model. Revisit sync if users demonstrate a need to train across devices.

---

❓ **Q2 — What do we owe people with Supabase templates?** If the hosted project contains templates someone relies on, should retiring it require a verified way for that person to keep them? What evidence would make you comfortable skipping migration?

➡️ **My recommendation:** Check what the hosted environment contains before deciding. If anyone relies on their templates, make a verified transfer path a condition of retirement. If the records are all disposable test data, skip migration.

---

❓ **Q3 — Is recovery part of the local-storage promise?** A user logs six months of workouts and loses their phone. Should the first release that stores real workout history already provide a way to back it up and restore it, or is that an acceptable limitation for the MVP?

➡️ **My recommendation:** Require manual export and import before people are expected to rely on the app as their workout history. An internal demo can ship earlier. Moving existing Supabase templates is a separate decision from protecting future on-device records.
